finding.certsh_data.ct_only: {count} name(s) appear in public certificates but do not resolve in DNS (retired environments or leaked internal names): {names}
module.certsh_data.checks: Lists the certificates issued for the domain and its subdomains from CT logs (crt.sh, Cert Spotter as a fallback): issuers, validity, wildcards, and names seen only in CT, absent from DNS.
module.certsh_data.fix:
Review each name flagged (present in a public certificate but missing from the DNS) and find the team, project or server that requested that certificate.
If nobody recognizes the name or the certificate (issuer, date): treat it as a certificate issued without your knowledge. Ask the issuing authority to revoke it, check access to your DNS and to your certificate issuance accounts (ACME, authority console), and change their passwords.
If the name matches a retired environment: revoke its certificate if it is still valid, disable its automatic renewal and delete its private key.
If the name is internal and has leaked (for example `intranet`, `vpn-paris`): publication in the logs is public and permanent, so check that the service it names is unreachable or protected. From now on, use an internal certificate authority for internal names, or a wildcard certificate that does not list each name.
Limit the authorities allowed to issue for your domain with a CAA record (module "Additional DNS records (CAA, SRV, TLSA)").
Monitor new certificates: subscribe to a Certificate Transparency log monitoring service with email alerts (the list of monitors is on the Certificate Transparency project site).
Check the list of public names with the command in the snippet, then run the scan again.
module.certsh_data.title: Public certificates (Certificate Transparency)
module.certsh_data.why: Every public certificate is visible to everyone: it reveals hostnames (internal ones included), the authorities used and certificates issued without the organisation's knowledge.
